client: I've been having a really hard time since my sister passed away six months ago. It was a car accident, and some days I can barely get out of bed because everything just feels so empty and pointless. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I guess I'm here because I don't know what else to do.
therapist: I'm so deeply sorry for the loss of your sister — what you're carrying sounds incredibly heavy, and the emptiness you're describing after such a sudden, traumatic loss makes complete sense. It takes real courage to show up here even when a part of you isn't sure it will help, and I want you to know that doubt is welcome here too. Can you tell me a little more about what your days have been feeling like lately?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, my days feel kind of hollow, like I'm just going through the motions. I wake up and for a split second everything feels normal, and then it hits me again that she's gone, and it's like the whole day just collapses before it even starts. I keep finding myself sitting in rooms not really knowing how I got there or what I was supposed to be doing.
therapist: That moment you describe — waking up and having that brief second of normalcy before the grief rushes back in — sounds like one of the most painful parts of the day, almost like losing her again and again each morning. The way you're drifting through spaces without knowing how you got there tells me your mind and body are really struggling under the weight of this. I'm wondering, in those hollow moments when you find yourself sitting somewhere, what kinds of thoughts tend to surface for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: It's usually this crushing guilt that hits me first — like, why didn't I call her more, why did I let weeks go by without checking in. And then my mind starts doing this awful thing where it replays specific moments, conversations I could have had differently, times I was too busy or too wrapped up in my own stuff to just be there for her. It's like my brain is determined to remind me that I failed her, even though I know somewhere deep down that's probably not entirely fair to myself.
therapist: That part of you that recognizes the guilt isn't entirely fair — that's an important voice, and I want us to hold onto it, because what you're describing sounds like your mind running a very harsh courtroom where you're both the accused and the only witness. Grief has a way of making our brains search desperately for *something* we could have controlled, as if finding fault in ourselves somehow makes the loss feel less random and terrifying. I'm curious — if your sister were here and could hear the way you've been speaking about yourself these past six months, what do you think she would say to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I've thought about that question before, actually, and it almost makes it worse somehow. She would probably tell me to stop beating myself up, that she loved me, that none of it was my fault — I know that's what she'd say. But knowing what she'd say and actually believing it feel like two completely different things, and I don't know how to close that gap.
therapist: You're describing something really profound — knowing something in your head and feeling it in your heart can feel like they're living in completely different worlds, and that gap can be one of the loneliest places to sit. As you said those words just now, I noticed something almost tender and fragile in the way you spoke, like this goes even deeper than the words themselves are letting on. I wonder — when you imagine her voice telling you she loves you and that it wasn't your fault, what happens inside you in that moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: When I try to imagine her saying that... I don't know, something in my chest just kind of tightens up, like my body is bracing for something. It almost feels wrong to let myself hear it, like I don't deserve to have that comfort, or like letting it in would mean I'm letting myself off the hook too easily. And then I feel guilty for even wanting it, which is just... exhausting.
therapist: What you just described — feeling guilty for even wanting comfort — is such a painful place to be trapped, like grief has set up a rule that says you have to keep suffering to prove you loved her enough. But I want to gently offer this: allowing yourself to receive her love isn't letting yourself off the hook, it's actually honoring the relationship you had with her. What do you think it would mean about you, or about her, if you did let that comfort in?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... but there's this voice in my head that says if I stop hurting, it means I've moved on, and moving on means I didn't love her enough. Like, what kind of person finds comfort when someone they loved is just gone? I don't know if I can separate "letting her love in" from "letting her go," because right now those feel like the exact same thing to me.
therapist: That belief — that love is proven through pain — is one of the most common and most cruel tricks grief plays on us, and it makes so much sense that your mind landed there. But I want to sit with something you said: what if carrying her love forward *is* how you keep her with you, rather than a way of leaving her behind? I'm wondering, is there anything about her — a value she had, something she believed in, a way she moved through the world — that you find yourself wanting to carry forward in your own life?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I sat with that for a second, and honestly... she was someone who never let people feel invisible. Like, she'd walk into a room and somehow notice the one person who looked like they were struggling, and she'd just go over and talk to them. I guess I've been so wrapped up in my own grief that I've kind of... pulled away from everyone, which feels like the opposite of who she was.
therapist: The way you just described her — someone who made people feel seen — there's so much love in that, and I notice something shifted as you spoke about her, like you were holding her very gently in that moment. And what you've recognized about yourself, that you've pulled away, doesn't sound like failure to me — it sounds like someone who is exhausted and hurting, but who still knows the way home. I'm wondering if honoring her gift, that ability to notice and reach toward people, might actually be one of the ways you keep her alive in the world — what feels true about that for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That actually... hit me somewhere I wasn't expecting. Like, I felt my chest tighten when you said "keep her alive in the world," because part of me wants that so badly, but another part of me wonders if I'm even capable of being that kind of person right now. I've been so closed off that I'm not sure I remember how to reach toward people without it feeling forced or hollow.
therapist: The way you just said that — softly, carefully — felt like someone touching something very fragile and real, and I want you to know that what you're feeling right now matters deeply. The fact that you *want* to be that person, that it tightens in your chest, tells me that capacity isn't gone — it's just buried under a lot of pain and exhaustion right now. I'm curious, is there one small, low-stakes moment you can imagine where you might let yourself reach toward just one person, not perfectly, not the way she did, but just... a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, but honestly, when I try to think of a specific person or moment, my mind just kind of goes blank and then immediately jumps to all the reasons it would go wrong. Like, what if I reach out and they're too busy, or they respond in a way that feels cold, and then I just feel more alone than before I tried? It almost feels safer to stay in this numb, closed-off place than to risk that.
therapist: What you're describing — that mental leap straight to everything that could go wrong — is your mind trying to protect you, but it's also keeping you in a kind of emotional hiding place where the pain feels manageable but connection feels impossible. That pattern of imagining the worst outcome before you've even taken a step is something we can really work with together, because right now it's making the risk feel much bigger than the reward. I'm wondering, has there ever been a time — even before your sister passed — where you reached out despite that fear and it turned out better than you expected?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... yeah, maybe once or twice. There was this coworker a few years back, I was nervous to ask her to grab lunch because I figured she'd think I was weird or just say no, and she actually seemed really happy I asked. But that feels different somehow — my sister dying changed something in me, like the stakes feel so much higher now when it comes to letting people in, because I already know exactly how much it hurts to lose someone you care about.
therapist: You just gave yourself really important evidence — that reaching out *can* go well, that people *can* surprise you — and even as you said it, there was something almost tender and quiet in your voice, like a small light you're not quite ready to trust yet. You're right that grief changes the stakes, because now you know loss in a way you didn't before, but I want to gently offer that the love you had with your sister is also proof that the risk of letting people in can be worth it. What would it mean to carry *that* piece of evidence — the coworker, the lunch — into the next time your mind tries to convince you it will only go wrong?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
